questions.stem: With [K⁺]out = 4 mM and [K⁺]in = 140 mM at 37 °C, what is the approximate K⁺ equilibrium potential?
questions.explanation: E_K = 61.5 × log(4/140) = 61.5 × (−1.54) ≈ −95 mV. A: The sign is wrong; [out] < [in] gives a negative log. B: 61 mV is the coefficient (and ≈ E_Na in magnitude), not the answer. D: −70 mV is the resting Vm, which also reflects Na⁺ and Cl⁻ permeability. E: Uses the divalent coefficient (30.75 mV, z = 2) instead of 61.5 mV.

questions.stem: A neuron rests at −70 mV although its E_K is about −95 mV. What best explains the difference?

options.A: A small resting Na⁺ permeability pulls Vm toward E_Na
options.B: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves equal charge each way
options.C: Resting Cl⁻ permeability exceeds K⁺ permeability
options.D: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated at rest
options.E: K⁺ is at electrochemical equilibrium at −70 mV

questions.explanation: Vm is a permeability-weighted average (GHK); P_K dominates, but resting P_Na is not zero, so Vm sits near, not at, E_K. B: The pump is electrogenic (3 Na⁺ out / 2 K⁺ in). C: P_K : P_Cl ≈ 1 : 0.45; K⁺ dominates. D: At rest Na⁺ channels are closed but available, not inactivated. E: At −70 mV K⁺ still has an outward driving force.

questions.stem: Shortly after an action potential, a nerve fiber fires again only if the stimulus is stronger than normal. What explains this?

options.A: Nearly all voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are still inactivated
options.B: E_Na has fallen because Na⁺ entry abolished the gradient
options.C: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is saturated after the action potential
options.D: Some Na⁺ channels have recovered, but K⁺ conductance is still high
options.E: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels are all closed

questions.explanation: This is the relative refractory period: partial Na⁺ channel recovery plus lingering K⁺ conductance means a stronger stimulus is needed. A: That is the absolute refractory period, when no stimulus works. B: One AP barely changes ion gradients; E_Na stays positive. C: The pump doesn't set refractoriness. E: K⁺ conductance is elevated, not zero.

questions.stem: A researcher holds a squid axon's membrane at 0 mV and records the current needed to keep it there. After tetraethylammonium is applied internally, the late outward current disappears. Which current did TEA abolish, and what technique was used?

options.B: Ca²⁺ current, using a current clamp
options.C: Cl⁻ current, using a voltage clamp
options.D: Leak current, using a current clamp
options.E: K⁺ current, using a voltage clamp

questions.explanation: Voltage clamp fixes Vm and measures the injected current; internal TEA blocks K⁺ channels, removing the delayed outward K⁺ current. A: TTX blocks Na⁺ channels from outside and wasn't used. B: Holding voltage constant is voltage clamp, not current clamp. C: TEA blocks K⁺ channels, not Cl⁻ channels. D: Wrong technique, and TEA isn't a general leak blocker.

questions.stem: Compared with an action potential, an electrotonic (graded) potential:

options.B: Spreads faster but decays with distance
options.C: Spreads only forward because of refractoriness
options.D: Is regenerated at each patch of membrane

questions.explanation: Electrotonic potentials are conducted faster than APs but attenuate rapidly (decremental), so they suit local integration, not long-distance signaling. A: They have no fixed threshold. C: They can spread both ways; refractoriness applies to APs. D: Regeneration is what makes APs nondecremental. E: They can be depolarizing (Na⁺) or hyperpolarizing (Cl⁻).

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has K⁺ of 7.5 mEq/L and muscle weakness. What is the effect on his skeletal muscle resting membrane potential and excitability?

options.C: Depolarized; reduced excitability due to Na⁺ channel inactivation
options.E: Depolarized; increased excitability due to K⁺ channel inactivation

questions.explanation: High [K⁺]out makes E_K less negative → resting depolarization; sustained depolarization inactivates voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → reduced excitability and weakness. A: Hyperpolarization occurs in hypokalemia. B: Also describes hypokalemia. D: The pump can't offset a large ECF K⁺ rise. E: Reduced, not increased, excitability, via Na⁺ (not K⁺) channel inactivation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has demyelinated axon segments. Which change in the demyelinated internode explains slowed or blocked conduction?

options.A: Membrane resistance rises and capacitance falls
options.B: Membrane resistance falls and capacitance rises
options.C: Both membrane resistance and capacitance rise
options.D: Both membrane resistance and capacitance fall
options.E: Nodal Na⁺ channels become permanently inactivated

questions.explanation: Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance; losing it does the opposite, so local current leaks out and charges the membrane before reaching the next node. A: That is the effect of myelin, which speeds conduction. C, D: Myelin moves the two in opposite directions. E: The problem is internodal current loss, not nodal channel inactivation.

questions.stem: Pulmonary interstitial edema triples the alveolar–capillary diffusion distance, and lung disease halves the surface area. With an unchanged O₂ gradient, O₂ diffusion becomes what fraction of normal?
questions.explanation: Fick: J ∝ A·ΔC/Δx, so J changes by (1/2) × (1/3) = 1/6. B: Accounts only for the distance. C: Accounts only for the area. D: Treats the halved area as doubled. E: Inverts the relationship; thickness and area work in the opposite directions.

questions.stem: Two coupled neurons fire in near-perfect synchrony, and current injected into either one immediately changes the voltage of the other. Their connection most likely:

options.A: Uses ligand-gated channels on the postsynaptic cell
options.B: Requires voltage-gated Ca²⁺ entry to transmit
options.D: Has a delay of about a millisecond

questions.explanation: Gap junctions (connexons) couple cells directly: minimal delay, often bidirectional, synchronize groups of cells. A: Ligand-gated receptors belong to chemical synapses. B: Ca²⁺-triggered transmitter release is the chemical synapse. C: Amplification is possible at chemical synapses; gap junctions are passive. D: A millisecond-range delay is typical of chemical synapses.
